I am 65 years old, and I have farmed these 4.5 mu in Quzhou County for 40 years. My son works in a factory in Handan, so it is just my wife and me at home now. We are not young anymore, so I value reliability over gambling for record yields. I have a high school education, which means I can read seed labels and follow extension recommendations, but I also trust what my own eyes have taught me across four decades.

It is early October, and the wheat sowing window is open. I will rotary-till the entire 4.5 mu to break up the maize stubble and level the field for the seeder. I plant an improved wheat variety—*Jimai* or *Shannong* type—that I buy from the county supply shop every two years. I do not use hybrid wheat; it is too expensive and unnecessary here. For the basal dressing, I spread compound fertilizer before the last pass of the rotary tiller, and I topdress urea at green-up and jointing. Because I have my own well, I will irrigate four times: once after sowing to ensure germination, once before winter to protect against frost heaving, once at jointing, and once at heading. I spray herbicide shortly after emergence, and I watch for aphids and fusarium; if I see them, I spray once or twice more. I expect about 480 kg per mu from this plot if the spring does not turn bone-dry.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, there is no time to waste. I will no-till plant hybrid maize the same day or the next day using a direct-seeder. The county station pushes new hybrid seeds every year—*Zhengdan* or *Xianyu* series—and I buy them because the vigor is obvious. Maize needs less phosphorus because the wheat leaves residual fertility, but it needs nitrogen at the big-trumpet stage. I will irrigate twice: the first at the jointing or tasseling stage, and the second at grain filling, because summer rains are unreliable. One herbicide application at sowing and one insecticide spray during the growing season are enough. I expect about 550 kg per mu from the maize.

This double-cropping rhythm is the only way 4.5 mu can feed two people and leave a little cash for medicine and electricity. I do not chase extreme yields; I chase consistency.
